claim: the Rehabilitation Subcode (N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4) requires complete removal of any existing wood-shake covering — no recover-over — even where a 1- or 2-family re-roof needs no permit
suggestedFix: Scope the wood-shake tear-off rule to permitted work: 'When a roofing permit is triggered — commercial, multi-family, or structural work — the Rehabilitation Subcode (N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4) requires complete removal of any existing wood-shake covering, with no recover-over.' Remove the 'even where a 1- or 2-family re-roof needs no permit' clause.

claim: An NJ re-roof on a detached 1- or 2-family home is ordinary maintenance with no permit, but the Rehabilitation Subcode requires complete removal of existing wood-shake covering — no recover-over
suggestedFix: Decouple and scope: state that a detached 1-2 family re-roof is ordinary maintenance with no permit (5:23-2.7), and that the Rehab Subcode wood-shake tear-off (5:23-6.4) applies only once a permit is triggered (commercial/multi-family/structural).

claim: asphalt installs at $6.50–$11.00 per sq ft in NJ versus $10–$20+ for cedar, per Josten Roofing NJ pricing
suggestedFix: Change to 'per Josten Roofing and NHI Contractors NJ pricing' so the $10–$20+ cedar figure is correctly tied to NHI Contractors, matching detailedAnalysis[0].

claim: Several Essex County homes have switched from aged cedar to synthetic.
suggestedFix: Delete the sentence, or replace with a sourced product fact, e.g. 'Synthetic-shake products from DaVinci and CertainTeed are designed for ~40–50-year service per CertainTeed product literature.'

claim: IBHS-recognized impact-rated (Class 4) asphalt shingles add hail resistance, rating to 2 in. hail under the 2025 FORTIFIED standard
suggestedFix: Tie the 2-inch figure to the IBHS Impact-Resistant 'Excellent'/'Good' rating under the 2025 FORTIFIED standard without the 'Class 4' label, or present Class 4 separately as the UL 2218 impact class rather than as the FORTIFIED 2-inch criterion.

claim: fire-retardant treatment matters most in NJ's wooded Essex County towns where ember exposure is a real risk
suggestedFix: Drop the ember-risk assertion or requalify to a sourced framing — e.g., 'carriers weigh the untreated-cedar fire class (nonclassified/unrated per NAHB and the CSSB), so fire-retardant treatment can ease NJ insurance scrutiny' — without claiming Essex County ember exposure as fact.
